messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Clinical Vignette: Marco

Marco was twenty-three when he fled Caracas, but the city had already claimed something from him that no border crossing could retrieve. He had been working as a junior analyst for a tech startup when the protests turned violent—the kind of escalation that happened in hours rather than days. He was walking home from the office on a Tuesday afternoon when the first tear gas canister detonated three blocks away. The sound was a dull metallic *thump*, followed by screams that seemed to come from everywhere at once. He ran without thinking, his lungs burning, his eyes streaming, unsure if he was being chased or if the chaos itself was chasing him. A motorcycle swerved toward the crowd and he threw himself against a storefront, certain in that moment that he would die on a street whose name he had walked a hundred times before. The bike passed. He made it home. But the relief lasted only until the next day, when his hands began to shake during a meeting and he couldn't stop seeing the blur of the motorcycle's headlight, couldn't stop hearing that sound.

By the time he arrived in Miami six weeks later, Marco had already begun the work of trying to survive what had happened. His body had become a stranger to him—constantly tense, muscles locked as though bracing for impact that never came. He would lie awake at night feeling his heart race, convinced something was wrong with him, and he'd press his fingers against his neck to count his pulse, run his hands down his ribs checking for wounds he knew weren't there. He started a new job as a Product Manager at a software company in Brickell, and for the first three weeks he managed to pass as functional. But then a colleague rolled his chair backward suddenly during a standup meeting, and Marco's entire body seized. He flinched so violently that everyone stopped talking. His face burned. He excused himself to the bathroom and didn't come back for twenty minutes.

The hypervigilance never truly left him. At the office, Marco found himself unable to focus on his laptop screen because part of his attention was always elsewhere—monitoring the movements of people around him, tracking who came in and out of the conference room, noting exits and open spaces. His manager commented that he seemed "distracted." What Marco experienced was something closer to a constant state of readiness, a vigilance so consuming that it felt like his body was running a program he couldn't shut down. Every unexpected sound made him flinch. A door closing too quickly, a raised voice from another team, the metallic *ding* of the elevator arriving—each one sent a jolt through his nervous system that felt indistinguishable from actual danger.

It was this relentless state of alert that drove him to begin hurting himself. Not dramatically, not in ways that left permanent marks, but with deliberate intention. He would pinch the skin on his inner arm until it bruised, or press his fingernails into his palm hard enough to leave crescents of white before the blood returned. The pain was clarifying in a way nothing else was—it gave him something real to focus on, something he could control and understand, and it seemed to break the cycle of his body's constant vigilance, at least for a few minutes. It was as though his nervous system had so much energy trapped inside it that physical pain was the only release valve. After he hurt himself, his muscles would relax slightly, his breathing would slow. The temporary relief was powerful enough that he began doing it more often—in his apartment after work, in the bathroom stall at the office, sometimes just before bed when the anxiety felt like it might swallow him whole.

But the relief never lasted. Within hours, sometimes within minutes, the tension would rebuild. His body would resume its state of high alert, scanning for threats, waiting for something terrible to happen. And because he was hurting himself, his body monitoring intensified—he became hyperaware of any pain or sensation, constantly checking his arms and hands for marks, worried that someone would see them and ask questions he couldn't answer. He also began seeking reassurance obsessively, texting friends late at night asking if they thought he was "okay," if something seemed "wrong" with him, if they noticed he seemed "off." His best friend from high school eventually stopped responding to these messages. Marco's own vigilance had taught him to interpret silence as confirmation that something was indeed very wrong.

He came to therapy after his manager pulled him aside and suggested he might benefit from "support." Marco sat across from the clinician with his hands folded tightly in his lap, and when asked what brought him in, he said only: "I don't feel safe in my own body anymore." What he meant was that the line between the war zone and his present life had blurred so completely that he could no longer tell the difference between a real threat and the ghost of one. His body was still running the program it had learned in Caracas, and nothing he did—not the pain, not the reassurance, not the checking—seemed to convince it that he was actually safe.
